title: I Have Cut the Cords of Hope That Bound Me to You
intro: Abu al-Atahiya addresses the world like a travelling companion he has done with. Shukri Faisal records a tradition connecting the opening with Utba, the woman the poet courted. In the surviving poem it is the world he names, and what he studies first is the evidence of his own ageing. A vision of judgement gives way to the daily cost of asking someone a favour and to the simple act of untying a camel.

translation: I have cut the cords of hope that bound me to you
and lifted my saddles down from the camels’ backs.
1.sharh: The travelling equipment is real enough to handle. Only in the next verse will he tell us that the companion whose ties he has cut is this world.

translation: I have given up hope of living to enjoy what I have gained
from you, world, or of having it last as long as I do.
2.sharh: He tries the question in both directions. To take lasting pleasure in a possession he would need security for two lives, his own and that of the thing possessed.

translation: I have felt the coolness of giving up hope inside my ribs,
and I have done with camping and setting out.
3.sharh: Despair has a surprisingly pleasant temperature. Giving up the chase releases him from the business of making camp as well as from setting off again.

translation: If I did hope, how many a flash of rainless lightning
has gleamed for hungry eyes, how many a glint of mirage.
4.sharh: Lightning usually promises rain and a mirage looks like water already on the ground. His hopes misled him through two different, perfectly familiar kinds of shine.

translation: What an unlucky time, when hope of you was killing me
and the daughters of your promise wrestled in my mind.
5.sharh: A single promise has offspring, all the possibilities a man begins to imagine. They jostle for space in his mind even before anything has been given to him.

translation: Now, world, I know you. Go your way,
home of everything that scatters and passes.
6.sharh: Calling the world a home sets up an expectation of permanence. All that actually lives in this house, he says, is dispersal and loss.

translation: Now time has become my tutor,
visiting morning and evening with its examples.
7.sharh: Time calls on him twice a day. Its lessons come as examples, the things he can actually see happening, and age has finally made him teachable.

translation: Now I see the road to right guidance.
My energies are free of their old preoccupations.
8.sharh: On the third “now” a road becomes visible. The obstacle that has lifted is the multitude of errands on which his own attention used to be sent.

translation: Grey hair has stationed its heralds of death for me.
It gets word to me at crown and nape.
9.sharh: A death announcement ordinarily reaches the survivors. Grey hair delivers his own in advance, by two sites on his head where it has begun to show.

translation: I have seen death, its sword flashing
in the hand of doom wherever I face.
10.sharh: The flash recalls the deceptive lightning of the opening. This gleam makes a promise he does believe, and changing his position does nothing to put it out of sight.

translation: I have seen the ties of life fray through.
The heirs have already set their sights on my wealth.
11.sharh: Life hangs by loops that can wear through one by one. His heirs need no such image to recognise an approaching change of ownership.

translation: I have seen proofs that things perish
in the unfamiliar turns my own condition takes.
12.sharh: His own circumstances have become strange to him. That small shock of no longer recognising oneself supplies evidence for a much larger claim.

translation: When I take heed, I see events descend,
running their course with livelihoods and lifespans.
13.sharh: Events alight and then run on. They carry both a person's provision and the time in which it can be enjoyed, two things the owner cannot arrange to suit himself.

translation: When men reckon up their pedigrees, I see
no lineage to match good deeds.
14.sharh: Pedigree is usually established by naming one's forebears. The poet enters good conduct in the same contest, though that is something an ancestor cannot do on one’s behalf.

translation: When I look for a God-fearing man, I find
a man whose deeds bear out his words.
15.sharh: His search has a practical test. The deed comes after the spoken claim and serves as the witness that makes it credible.

translation: When someone fears God and obeys Him,
you see him among noble deeds and high things.
16.sharh: A private disposition becomes recognisable through conduct. The shift to “you see” lets the listener try the preceding test for himself.

translation: When the devout man takes firm root in devotion,
two crowns are his, tranquillity and dignity.
17.sharh: The two crowns distinguish inward composure from the dignity visible to other people. Nothing in this ceremonial dress needs to be bought or inherited.

translation: Night goes, and day, each taking a turn
carrying creation through retreat and approach.
18.sharh: Night and day take turns over the same creatures. Each brings the other back, but the people handed from one to the next do not get back the time they have spent.

translation: For anyone whose own death is being announced, enough
are the days and nights that have gone by.
19.sharh: No one has to pronounce a name. The days a person can already count as past constitute enough of an announcement that his own life is passing.

translation: Cast your eye wherever you please. You stand amid
lessons coming hard upon one another.
20.sharh: There is no privileged place to look. What asks for attention is the rate at which one instance overtakes another, wherever a person happens to turn.

translation: The new wears out while you are still renewing it.
Everything you have made new will wear out too.
21.sharh: Decay need not wait for the repairs to finish. The repeated forms of “new” make audible how often the owner starts the same work again.

translation: You there, complacent in your good fortune, tomorrow
your limbs will lie scattered in your grave.
22.sharh: The sentence spans a turn from public self-importance to a body coming apart in private. “Tomorrow” allows the addressee no comfortable interval in between.

translation: The man in earnest for guidance cuts his wishes short.
Yours, I see, have long trailing hems.
23.sharh: A person ready for work tucks up his garment. The other man has dressed his hopes in so much trailing cloth that they will trip him up.

translation: Seldom will you find a worse cheat of his own soul
than one who toys with it, merry and proud.
24.sharh: The merriment is genuine enough at the moment it is felt. The fraud lies in persuading oneself that treating a life as a toy can have no lasting cost.

translation: Dealer in error, trading to your judgement’s loss,
how long will you bid so high for error?
25.sharh: He bids up the price of the very commodity that damages his ability to value things. The trade costs him his judgement before it costs him anything else.

translation: Praise to God, praiseworthy for His bounty.
The idler’s hand has lost its stake and made no gain.
26.sharh: The thanksgiving breaks into the trader’s reckoning. God's gift is acknowledged at the very point where the idler’s supposedly profitable business shows a loss.

translation: God has a day when their skin will shudder
and children’s forelocks turn white.
27.sharh: Grey hair previously gave an old man warning. Now it appears on children, recalling the children turned grey in Qur'an 73.17 and making ordinary ageing seem mercifully slow.

translation: A day of calamities and earthquakes, when pregnant women
cast out what they carry.
28.sharh: The earthquake reaches even the protected space of the womb. The image of pregnancies brought abruptly to an end recalls the opening of Qur'an 22.

translation: A day of gains and losses, of separation and weighing,
of matters terrible in their consequence.
29.sharh: The day of mutual loss and gain is a Qur'anic name for judgement. The next two nouns add parting and weighing, as if the final accounts were being taken in several stages.

translation: A day when every soul led astray is summoned
to garments cut from fire and to fetters.
30.sharh: The punishment fits like clothing cut to measure, an echo of the fire-garments of Qur'an 22.19. The fetters complete an outfit the wearer has no power to remove.

translation: For the devout there is a welcome laid on in honour.
A fresh radiance and beauty rise upon their faces.
31.sharh: A host’s first provisions for a guest are ready before the arrival. We see the welcome taking effect in the guests’ faces.

translation: Companies whose faces light up for the reckoning
shine and sparkle there.
32.sharh: The groups can be distinguished by the light their faces give off. A poem that began with a delusive flash can now imagine a brightness worthy of trust.

translation: White-blazed racers with white stockings run ahead,
their bellies lean, their burdens light.
33.sharh: Their markings are those of fine horses, and the religious image of luminous faces and limbs is close at hand. The meagre diet and light burden will belong to human beings in the next verse.

translation: Among them are the unkempt, once dusty and thin,
in worn cloaks and patched shirts.
34.sharh: The account looks back from their brilliance at judgement to their former appearance. A patched shirt might once have made precisely these people easy to overlook.

translation: They come as guests to the most generous Master, who shelters them
in a royal dwelling of majesty and shade.
35.sharh: The earlier promise of hospitality now has a host and a dwelling. Its royalty is made tangible through something a tired guest can feel, the shelter of shade.

translation: The son of Adam has many a device for his affairs.
Death cuts short the schemer’s last device.
36.sharh: Human ingenuity gets a plural in the first half. Death needs one verb to put an end to the inventor and to whatever invention he had in hand.

translation: Among those who tell Adam’s son of his own death
are moving feet and the rise of every new moon.
37.sharh: The two clocks are of quite different sizes, a footfall and a lunar month. Both perform the office of the herald who announced the poet’s death in his grey hair.

translation: Why do I see you wearing away your unblemished face?
World, you have worn out the faces of men.
38.sharh: The face is what a petitioner must present to another person. Having to do so over and over wears down standing and self-respect as surely as use wears through cloth.

translation: I weighed what it costs to ask. Its value exceeded
that of any kindness obtained by asking.
39.sharh: The favour has a price even if the giver charges nothing. He puts a value on what the petitioner has already had to spend in making the request.

translation: Keep a tighter grip upon your request
than the man who keeps his money from you.
40.sharh: The petitioner too has something he can refuse to part with. His reserve in asking might outdo the wealthy man's reserve in giving.

translation: Guard your good name as well as you can.
It outweighs the bestowal of every gift.
41.sharh: The scales return, this time to weigh reputation against the benefits a gift might bring. The heavier object is the one nobody can put in a purse.

translation: I marvel at the man intent on growing his money.
The accumulator forgets the grace of having little.
42.sharh: The investor knows how to draw fruit from money. He overlooks a kind of elegance available precisely to those who possess little.

translation: If a man tangles his resolve up in doubts,
he takes the road on the young camel of error.
43.sharh: Doubt does not necessarily leave a person at a standstill. He is moving quite briskly in the picture, carried along by a riding camel he should never have mounted.

translation: When the tricks of fortune call out,
the places where champions fell bear witness for them.
44.sharh: Fortune calls, and the ground on which heroes fell gives evidence about the caller. Even the strongest men have left records of having been taken in.

translation: If need drives you to offer your face as a suppliant,
offer it to someone gracious and generous.
45.sharh: He makes room for a need too pressing for self-sufficiency. The right person to approach will understand what is at stake in being seen to ask.

translation: If you fear your way is blocked in a town,
grasp with both hands the chance to leave at once.
46.sharh: The opening traveller unpacked his saddles. Packing up again makes sense now, if a change of place can spare someone an intolerable dependence.

translation: Be patient with the reversals of time.
Relief from distress is like untying a hobble.
47.sharh: A thin rope can keep an entire camel still. After a poem concerned with the long wait for release, it takes only the movement of a hand to give the animal back its stride.

1.1.3.head: حَبيلَة
1.1.3.meaning: Cords or snares. Hopes supply the ties that attach him to the world.

1.2.5.head: رَحل
1.2.5.meaning: The saddle and travelling gear carried on a camel.

2.1.5.head: نالَ
2.1.5.meaning: Obtained something one had been seeking.

3.1.2-3.head: بَرد اليَأس
3.1.2-3.meaning: “The coolness of despair.” The relief that comes when one has given up an anxious hope.

3.1.5.head: جانِحَة
3.1.5.meaning: The ribs, enclosing the place where he feels relief.

3.2.3.head: حِلّ
3.2.3.meaning: Coming to a halt and making camp.

4.1.5.head: خُلَّب
4.1.5.meaning: Lightning followed by no rain, a familiar figure for an empty promise.

4.2.5.head: آل
4.2.5.meaning: A shimmering mirage mistaken from afar for water.

5.2.1-2.head: بَنات الوَعد
5.2.1-2.meaning: “Daughters of your promise.” The hopes one promise breeds in its hearer.

5.2.3.head: اِعتَلَجَ
5.2.3.meaning: To jostle and contend, here within a person's thoughts.

7.1.5.head: مُؤَدِّب
7.1.5.meaning: A tutor entrusted with forming a person's habits as well as teaching him.

7.2.1.head: غَدا
7.2.1.meaning: Came in the morning. Its companion verb describes an evening visit.

8.2.2.head: هِمَّة
8.2.2.meaning: Aims and energies directed towards an end.

9.1.5.head: ناعٍ
9.1.5.meaning: A herald who announces a death. Grey hairs have been appointed to the office.

9.2.3.head: مَفرِق
9.2.3.meaning: The parting of the hair on top of the head.

9.2.4.head: قَذال
9.2.4.meaning: The back of the head just above the neck.

10.2.5.head: حِيال
10.2.5.meaning: Opposite me, in my line of sight.

11.1.3.head: عُروَة
11.1.3.meaning: Loops or fastenings, the points by which a life holds together.

11.1.5.head: تَخَرَّمَ
11.1.5.meaning: Broke or wore through at the points of fastening.

13.1.4.head: حَطّ
13.1.4.meaning: Alighting or descending, here of events bearing their allotments.

13.2.3.head: أَجَل
13.2.3.meaning: The allotted spans of people's lives or the ends of those spans.

15.2.4.head: فِعال
15.2.4.meaning: By actual conduct, offered as evidence for a person's words.

17.1.4.meaning: Took deep root or became a settled habit.

18.1.4.head: تَعاوُر
18.1.4.meaning: By turns, each succeeding the other.

19.1.3.head: نَعى
19.1.3.meaning: To announce a death. Here the living man receives his own notice.

20.1.2.head: طَرف
20.1.2.meaning: One's gaze, sent roaming to see what it can find.

20.2.3.head: تَدارُك
20.2.3.meaning: Catching up, of one lesson close on the heels of another.

21.2.5.head: بالٍ
21.2.5.meaning: Destined to wear out, even while it looks new.

22.1.3.head: بَطِر
22.1.3.meaning: Made heedless or overbearing by prosperity.

22.2.4.head: وَصل
22.2.4.meaning: The joined parts of the body, its limbs and joints.

23.1.4.head: مُشَمِّر
23.1.4.meaning: Someone in earnest, literally a person with clothing tucked up for work.

23.2.4.head: ذَيل
23.2.4.meaning: Trailing hems that can hinder the wearer's movement.

24.1.4.head: أَغَرّ
24.1.4.meaning: More deceptive, with the added sting that the victim is himself.

25.2.5.head: غالى
25.2.5.meaning: To overbid or carry something to excess. Both senses suit the trader.

26.2.5.head: بَطّال
26.2.5.meaning: An idler who spends life on what brings no real return.

27.2.3.head: ذُؤابَة
27.2.3.meaning: Locks of hair, startlingly grey on children.

28.1.2.head: نازِلَة
28.1.2.meaning: Grave afflictions that descend on people.

28.2.5.head: حَمل
28.2.5.meaning: The unborn children cast forth in the terror of judgement.

29.1.2.head: تَغابُن
29.1.2.meaning: The disclosure of ultimate loss and gain, a Qur'anic name for Judgement Day.

29.1.3.head: تَبايُن
29.1.3.meaning: The parting of destinies at judgement.

30.2.1.head: مُقَطَّعات
30.2.1.meaning: Garments cut to fit their wearers, here made of fire.

30.2.3.head: غُلّ
30.2.3.meaning: Fetters or an iron collar used in binding someone.

31.1.3.head: نُزُل
31.1.3.meaning: A provision of hospitality prepared for an arriving guest.

31.2.3.head: نَضرَة
31.2.3.meaning: Freshness or radiance visible in the face.

32.2.4.head: تَلالي
32.2.4.meaning: Sparkling or repeatedly flashing. The usual hamza is softened in the rhyme.

33.1.2.head: أَغَرّ
33.1.2.meaning: White-blazed, like a horse marked on the forehead.

33.1.3.head: مُحَجَّلَة
33.1.3.meaning: White-stockinged, of the lower legs of a horse.

33.2.1-2.head: خُمص البُطون
33.2.1-2.meaning: “Hollow-bellied.” Lean from scant eating or training.

34.2.4.head: سِربال
34.2.4.meaning: A shirt or long garment worn on the body.

35.1.4.head: أَظَلَّ
35.1.4.meaning: Gave them shade and shelter, as a host receives guests from the heat.

36.1.1.head: حيلَة
36.1.1.meaning: Devices or expedients for getting one's way.

36.1.6.head: كَثير
36.1.6.meaning: Numerous. Both editions and the reciter’s caption give “many”, set against the one death that defeats every scheme. The consonant could also be heard as «كبيرة», “great”.

37.2.1-2.head: حَرَك الخُطى
37.2.1-2.meaning: “The movement of footsteps.” A bodily measure of passing time.

37.2.5.head: هِلال
37.2.5.meaning: The new crescent, marking the passage of another lunar month.

38.1.4-5.head: حُرّ الوَجه
38.1.4-5.meaning: “The noble part of your face.” The dignity one risks in making a request.

38.1.6.head: مُخلِق
38.1.6.meaning: Wearing something thin, as a garment wears through.

39.2.3.head: عارِفَة
39.2.3.meaning: A favour or act of kindness.

40.1.5.head: ضَنانَة
40.1.5.meaning: Reluctance to part with something valued.

41.1.2.head: مَحمَدَة
41.1.2.meaning: Praiseworthy qualities and the good name they earn.

42.1.4.head: مُثَمِّر
42.1.4.meaning: Someone who makes his wealth yield an increase.

42.2.4.head: إِقلال
42.2.4.meaning: Having little in the way of possessions.

43.1.3.head: لَبَسَ
43.1.3.meaning: To mix things up or confound them.

43.2.4.head: قَعود
43.2.4.meaning: A young camel old enough to ride.

44.2.3.head: مَصرَع
44.2.3.meaning: The places where men fell, made witnesses to the workings of fortune.

45.1.3-4.head: بَذل الوَجه
45.1.3-4.meaning: “Offering your face.” Exposing one's dignity in asking for help.

46.1.3.head: تَعَذُّر
46.1.3.meaning: A difficulty that closes off the means of livelihood.

46.2.3.head: عاجِل
46.2.3.meaning: Immediate. Both editions urge the traveller to leave without delay. The recording could also be heard as «بعادل», “just” or “fair”, which gives the journey no clear description here.

47.2.5.head: عِقال
47.2.5.meaning: A hobble that holds a camel's folded foreleg, released by undoing its knot.
